title: Weekend cabin
topic: A friend is closing out the cabin and grocery money in the group chat
blurb: A friend is wrapping up the weekend cabin expenses in the group chat.
prompt: A friend just texted this in the group chat. If one line doesn't add up, tap it.

segments.label: The room
segments.text: Three of us got a cabin for the weekend. I put the $600 room on my card — $200 each.

segments.label: The groceries
segments.text: Mia also grabbed groceries for everyone, $90.

segments.label: The settle-up
segments.text: That's $30 each for food, so Mia sent me $170 and Jake sent me $230. We're even.

segments.label: The receipt
segments.text: I'll drop the receipt in the chat in case anyone wants it.

conclusion: Mia sent $170 and Jake sent $230, so the cabin and the groceries are all even.

flaws.original: Jake's $30 for groceries should go to Mia, not me. Mia should send me $140 for the room, not $170.
flaws.corrupted: That's $30 each for food, so Mia sent me $170 and Jake sent me $230. We're even.

diagnosis_choices.label: Jake's $30 for groceries went to you, not Mia. She paid $260 and you paid $200 — she just bought your dinner.
The $90 groceries should have been split four ways, because you also bought snacks on the drive.
Jake still owes $10, because $600 plus $90 is $690, and $230 plus $170 is only $400.

fix_choices.label: Send Mia the $30 Jake gave you, or have her send you $140 instead of $170.
Ask Jake for another $30 so Mia can be paid back from a new transfer.
Let Mia keep a larger share of the cabin, which cancels the groceries on her side only.

flaws.explanation: Jake's $30 for groceries went into your pocket, not Mia's. She just bought your dinner.
flaws.why_tempting: Take $30 off one transfer, add $30 to the other, and the two numbers look perfectly netted. The grocery money just landed with the wrong person.
flaws.catch_rule: When you net two bills, follow each person's share to the person who actually paid that bill.
flaws.hint: Who paid for the groceries? And who ended up with Jake's $30?

practice.problem: You paid a $120 ride for three people. Lin paid $30 for parking. Lin sends you $30 and Sam sends you $50, and you call it even. What's wrong?
practice.answer: Sam's $10 parking share went to you, not Lin. Lin should have sent $20, or you should pass Sam's $10 along.

clean_segments: Three of us got a cabin for the weekend. I put the $600 room on my card — $200 each.
Mia also grabbed groceries for everyone, $90.
Jake's $30 for groceries should go to Mia, not me. Mia should send me $140 for the room, not $170.
I'll drop the receipt in the chat in case anyone wants it.
clean_conclusion: Jake's grocery share should go to Mia. She owes you $140 for the room, not $170.

diagnosis: The room bill should be split only between the two people who did not pay up front.
Each guest owes the entire room price.
Mia’s groceries are included in the $600 room charge.
fix: Use $300 as each guest’s room share.
Assign $600 of room cost to each guest.
Deduct the $90 groceries from the room price first.

diagnosis: The $90 is already a per-person cost.
Mia’s grocery share is zero because she paid.
The groceries were bought for only the two people who did not pay.
fix: Exclude Mia from her own share of the groceries.
Divide the grocery cost between the other two guests only.
